content: Our right to bodily autonomy is under constant threat. Practices that directly or indirectly influence our choices—such as the treatment we receive from healthcare providers, access to antiretroviral (ARV) treatment options, or contraceptive choices—undermine human rights and have severe consequences for our mental and physical health, as well as every aspect of our lives. Svitlana Moroz highlights how slogans like 90-90-90 and Getting to Zero, often promoted by UN agencies, fail to address the social determinants of health-seeking behavior. She explains that women living with HIV face the challenge of convincing society and policymakers about the intersectionality of deprivation, violence, and community health. She emphasizes that addressing HIV requires sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and gender equality as foundational starting points. Cecilia points out that current policies continue to marginalize vulnerable communities, including immigrants, people of color, and transgender individuals. L’Orangelis adds that discussions in clinics should not solely focus on protecting others from HIV. Many women face sexual violence and coercion, yet gender-sensitive perspectives are still absent in many healthcare services. Dorothy describes progress in Kenya, where women advocates are now welcomed by healthcare providers and are actively involved in community committees addressing their SRHR. This marks a significant shift, as advocates are both recipients and providers of care, working collaboratively with healthcare staff. In the United States, Cecilia explains the success of a participatory process led by the community, where researchers are invited to learn about the needs and interests of women living with HIV. This approach has improved relationships between researchers, funders, and communities, with more funders now supporting transgender-led organizations. In Ukraine, Svitlana and her team collected 40 stories from women living with HIV, showcasing both positive experiences of health support and the damaging effects of stigma and discrimination within the healthcare system. In Latin America and Southern Africa, L’Orangelis focuses on empowering women living with HIV to understand and advocate for the implementation of SRHR policies, ensuring that these policies translate into tangible benefits in their lives. Healthcare providers and policymakers are beginning to recognize the importance of involving women living with HIV in decisions that affect their lives. This meaningful involvement not only upholds their intrinsic rights but also leads to better health outcomes for all. Women living with HIV have the right to full SRHR services, including access to prevention, care, treatment, and support for reproductive organ cancers and assisted reproductive technologies. Sexual rights include the freedom to decide if, when, and with whom to engage in sexual experiences, as well as the right to explore one’s own body and sexuality. Reproductive rights encompass the ability to make informed decisions about starting a family, including the number and timing of children, and access to contraception and birthing methods. Dorothy Onyango, CEO of Women Fighting AIDS in Kenya (WOFAK), emphasizes that healthcare providers need guidance on gender and human rights to better address the needs of women living with HIV. WOFAK, established in 1994, has grown significantly and contributes to Kenya’s national HIV response, providing comprehensive care and support for women, youth, and children affected by HIV.
